name: Internationalism
summary: Internationalism holds that peace and prosperity depend on cooperation among states and peoples rather than national rivalry. Its liberal strand (Kant, Cobden, Hobson, Angell, Wilson, the League and the UN) wants open diplomacy, arbitration, reduced armaments, collective security and open trade, and rejects conquest and annexation; its proletarian strand (the International Working Men's Association, Basel, Zimmerwald) calls for working-class solidarity across borders and peace without annexations. Both back self-determination and oppose chauvinism.
scope: Mainstream liberal internationalism from Kant's Perpetual Peace and the Cobden-Bright tradition through Hobson, Angell, Wilson's Fourteen Points, the League Covenant, the Atlantic Charter and the UN Charter, with the proletarian strand (the First International, Basel, Zimmerwald) as the documented alternative. Answers rest only on what these texts and the scholarship on them state about relations among states and peoples, and on the UN's own rights texts where the Charter charges the organisation with them; domestic economic, cultural and moral questions are null unless a text settles them. Excludes anarchist, fascist and cultural internationalisms and the wider camps of liberalism, socialism and human-rights doctrine.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Hobson argues that a durable peace needs an international council with executive power, an arbitral court and in the last resort an international force, and Wilson's fourteenth point and the Covenant create a general association of nations to guarantee peace.

nation-first.rationale: Wilson says the world's peace programme is his own and that unless justice is done to others it will not be done to us; Mazzini ranks duties to Humanity before those to country, and the International's rules call emancipation neither a local nor a national problem.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Hobson accepts that states must give up part of their sovereignty to an international council with legislative and enforcing power, but Kant wants only a non-coercive league and the Covenant and Charter keep sovereign equality and a right to withdraw.

free-trade.rationale: Cobden, Hobson and Wilson hold that free trade is a great peacemaker that serves all nations, while Marx votes for free trade only because it hastens social revolution and says it does not help workers.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Wilson's third point calls for removing economic barriers, Cobden's programme is complete freedom of trade, Hobson calls the fallacies and injuries of protectionism something to expose, and Marx votes for free trade over the conservative protective system.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Kant and Cobden bar armed interference in another state's affairs, while scholarship counts humanitarian intervention among the liberal-internationalist policies of the 1990s; the Charter itself allows Chapter VII enforcement against domestic jurisdiction.

non-intervention.rationale: Kant's fifth preliminary article and Cobden's non-intervention principle forbid interference, but liberal internationalism in practice includes humanitarian and enforcement action, and the Charter's domestic-jurisdiction clause carves out Chapter VII.

force-without-un.rationale: The Charter bans the threat or use of force except in self-defence or under Security Council authority, and scholarship treats a US turn to unilateralism and illegal force as abandoning liberal internationalism.

collective-defense.rationale: Under the Covenant a member that goes to war in breach of its terms is deemed to have committed an act of war against all members, which undertake to guarantee each other's territorial integrity, and the Charter recognises collective self-defence.

arms-reduction.rationale: Wilson's fourth point, Article 8 of the Covenant, the Atlantic Charter and Cobden's programme all call for national armaments to be cut to the lowest level consistent with safety.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Internationalist texts ask for armaments to be reduced to the lowest point consistent with national safety, not abolished, and the Charter has members supply armed forces to the Security Council.

military-superiority.rationale: Cobden's programme renounces national preponderance and supremacy and Kant and the Covenant treat arms races as a cause of war, but Angell grants that states must keep up their relative strength while the old philosophy lasts.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Wilson says the day of conquest and aggrandizement is gone, the Atlantic Charter disclaims any aggrandizement, Cobden's programme abandons conquest, Kant forbids absorbing states and Angell argues conquest does not pay.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The Atlantic Charter accepts no territorial change against the freely expressed wishes of the peoples concerned, and Kant and the Zimmerwald manifesto condemn annexation without consent.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: The Atlantic Charter wants territorial changes only in accord with the peoples' freely expressed wishes, though it does not say how those are to be expressed.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Zimmerwald manifesto calls the right of self-determination of nations an indestructible principle, the Charter makes self-determination of peoples a purpose of the United Nations, and the Atlantic Charter affirms every people's right to choose its government.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Wilson's first point demands open covenants openly arrived at, Article 18 of the Covenant makes unregistered treaties non-binding, Kant bars treaties with secret reservations, and the Basel and Zimmerwald texts attack secret diplomacy.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Kant forbids violent interference in another state's constitution, the Charter bans force against any state's independence, and the Internationals condemn dynastic and great-power armed ventures.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Hobson wants international law and public right to replace private force and the Covenant requires members to carry out arbitral awards in good faith, so national law does not have the last word.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Scholarship on liberal internationalism reports its advocates criticising the US for not accepting responsibility to help the world's poorest and records bipartisan support for economic and development aid.

delink-world-market.rationale: The Atlantic Charter wants all states, great or small, to have equal access to trade and raw materials, and Wilson and Hobson call for removing economic barriers and open commerce, which is the opposite of cutting economic ties.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Hobson's open-door doctrine says colonies should be the world's and that no state would envy another its colonies, and Wilson's third point and the Atlantic Charter seek equal trade conditions for all nations.

democratic-peace.rationale: Kant's first definitive article makes republican constitutions the first condition of perpetual peace, and scholarship on Kant presents wars among liberal states as the evidence.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Lenin and the Zimmerwald manifesto trace the war to capitalist imperialism, while Cobden and Angell hold that commerce makes for peace and conquest does not pay; Hobson ties imperialism to capitalist distribution but not as inevitable.

workers-nation.rationale: The International's rules found the emancipation of labour on fraternal union of the working classes of different countries, and the Manifesto, Basel and Zimmerwald texts call on proletarians of all countries to unite.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Article 22 of the Covenant entrusts peoples not yet able to stand alone to the tutelage of advanced nations as a sacred trust, while Kant condemns European conduct in colonial lands and the Zimmerwald manifesto condemns subjugation of weaker nations.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Article 73 of the Charter makes the interests of the inhabitants of non-self-governing territories paramount, Wilson's fifth point gives their interests equal weight with the ruling government's claims, and Hobson says colonies should be the world's.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Charter's preamble affirms the dignity and worth of the human person and the equal rights of men and women, and the Declaration's first article says all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Declaration gives everyone the right to take part in government on universal and equal suffrage without distinction of sex, and the Covenant opens League posts equally to men and women.

property-franchise.rationale: Rested only on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, an adjacent text, not internationalism's own.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Declaration requires universal and equal suffrage and bars distinctions of race, colour or national origin; the International admits members without regard to colour, creed or nationality.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Charter commits the UN to respect for human rights without distinction as to race, and the Declaration bars discrimination and promises equal protection against it.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Rested only on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, an adjacent text, not internationalism's own.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The Declaration includes freedom to change one's religion and to manifest it in teaching and practice, and the Charter bars distinction as to religion.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Rested only on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, an adjacent text, not internationalism's own.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Rested only on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, an adjacent text, not internationalism's own.

party-controls-media.rationale: Rested only on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, an adjacent text, not internationalism's own.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Declaration says the will of the people is the basis of the authority of government, the Atlantic Charter respects every people's right to choose its government, and Kant says no right over a people is thinkable without the original contract.

separated-powers.rationale: Kant makes a republican constitution rest on separating the executive from the legislative power, with representation, as the first condition of peace.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Kant calls despotism the union of lawmaking and enforcement in one ruler and contrasts it with the republic, and the Declaration makes all equal before the law.

worker-ownership.rationale: The Inaugural Address praises co-operative factories as showing that large-scale production needs no class of masters employing hands, and calls hired labour a transitory form destined to give way to associated labour.
